analysis.one_liner: Replaces the 1872 Mining Law with royalties, permits, and cleanup money for hardrock mining on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees from April 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock mining on federal land still runs under an 1872 law that lets companies claim public land and take gold, copper, lithium, and other minerals without paying the government any share of the value. This bill would have replaced that system: companies would pay a royalty of 12.5% on new mines and 8% on existing ones (with exemptions for small miners), get permits with cleanup bonds, and be barred from sacred sites, wilderness areas, and roadless forests. A quarter of the new money would go to the states where the mining happens; the rest would fund cleanup of tens of thousands of abandoned mines that leak acid and heavy metals into western rivers.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently shoulder cleanup costs for abandoned mines; people who live near or use western public lands and waters; tribes whose sacred sites and traditional lands could be affected; and state governments, which would receive 25% of the new mining revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes the first-ever royalty on hardrock mining from federal land: 12.5% of gross value on new mines and at least 8% on existing operations, with an exemption for small miners.

Sends 25% of royalties, rents, and fees to the state where the mining occurs, with the rest deposited in a Hardrock Minerals Reclamation Fund for cleaning up abandoned mine land and responding to hazardous releases.

Closes parts of the public domain to new mining claims, prohibits new patents that would transfer federal land to private ownership, and bars mining in sacred sites, wilderness study areas, critical habitat, inventoried roadless areas, and wild and scenic river corridors.

Requires federal agencies to consult with Indian tribes before mineral activities that could substantially affect tribal lands or interests, and requires operations permits with financial assurance that reclamation will actually be paid for.

Sets a standard that mining must prevent 'undue degradation' of public lands and requires reclamation plans showing that water will not need treatment for carcinogens or toxins ten years after mine closure.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, which today pay no federal royalty on gold, copper, silver, lithium, and other hardrock minerals taken from federal land. They would owe royalties, claim maintenance fees, application rentals, and cleanup bonds, and would face a longer permitting process and new acreage limits on how much land any one company can control in a state.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The United States is trying to expand domestic supplies of lithium, copper, and other battery minerals; new royalties and an added permitting layer could raise the cost of domestic mining and slow projects, though the bill does let the Secretary cut royalties to 6.25% for minerals the Department of Energy classifies as strategic and critical.

Existing mines and claims get long transitions — up to 10 years for claims to convert to leases — so the reform would not change conditions at operating mines for years, and the royalty on existing operations would be at least 8% rather than 12.5%.

Small miners holding up to 10 claims with under $50,000 in annual mineral income would pay no royalties at all under small miners leases, a carve-out that critics of the 1872 law's loopholes argue can be structured around.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: mining companies would pay for the first time for minerals taken from public land, and the money would fund cleanup that taxpayers now cover. The cost is that domestic mining of battery and grid minerals becomes somewhat more expensive and slower to permit, at a moment when policymakers want more of it — a tension the bill only partly addresses with its discount for strategic minerals. The transition periods for existing mines soften the industry's immediate hit but also delay the public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and two subcommittees the day it was introduced, and no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on April 26, 2022, with 11 original cosponsors.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and the next day to the Energy and Mineral Resources and Indigenous Peoples subcommittees.
Nineteen Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which continue to extract gold, copper, lithium, and other minerals from federal land without paying a royalty under the 1872 law, and without the new cleanup obligations the bill would have imposed.

industries.note: The bill would end a 150-year arrangement in which companies pay no federal royalty on gold, copper, lithium, and other hardrock minerals taken from public land, and would add permitting, reclamation bonds, and acreage limits. The industry's interest in keeping royalty-free access runs directly against the public's interest in collecting a share of the value and funding mine cleanup.

Miners holding 10 or fewer claims with under $50,000 in annual mineral income are exempt from royalties and claim maintenance fees and get a special small miners lease. This protects hobbyist and small operators who could not absorb the new costs.

Higher royalties and a new permitting system could raise the cost and slow the pace of domestic lithium, copper, and other battery-mineral production. The bill offsets this by allowing royalties to be cut to 6.25% for minerals classified as strategic and critical.

industries.industry: Mine reclamation and environmental remediation contractors
industries.note: A new Hardrock Minerals Reclamation Fund, financed by royalties and fees, would pay for cleanup of abandoned mine land and hazardous releases, creating funded work for remediation firms and reducing hazards that ordinary people otherwise live near.
